decisions.summary: The report opens with one table of the window (minutes, blocking, each as a percentage of the working time) and one line per landed task; builder minutes are the builder's event-log span.
decisions.why: This is how the report is laid out. It keeps T243's percentages of working time ((i)) and the breakdown the GM asked for. The table and the lines are the coordinating session's task-line words, and they narrow nothing he asked.

decisions.summary: Every make land is a batch keyed (feature, 'second tier: <tasks>'), owned by no task, with one category in the window table and its own section of one line per batch.
decisions.why: This is the GM's second message nearly word for word: 'move batched landing stuff that happens as the second tier of checks into its own separate category rather than counting it against any individual task.' Under the two-tier trial a single-task make land is also the second tier, so keying every landing as a batch matches his words.

decisions.summary: A task's own table ends at its make carry, found through the pool's log. With no carry found it ends where the batch's first attempt starts, a labeled GUESS knob (Batch::from).
decisions.why: This puts the GM's second message into effect: the second tier's time is not counted against a task. The fallback is a stated default of the kind (l) allows ('it doesn't have to be 100% exact'), and it is labeled where it is used.

decisions.summary: GUESS defaults for the second tier's blocking. A gate blocks nothing while any task's own blocking work is in flight. It blocks the batch (never a task) (a) when the session waits on it alone, (b) when it runs in the foreground, and (c) through a repair. A builder dispatched with Blocks: none leaves the gate waited on alone.
decisions.why: Each part was judged on its own. (c) A repair stops the batch from landing until the repair is done, which is (l)'s 'waiting on it to be done before it can be started' exactly. (b) A foreground run holds the session's next step by construction. (a) This is the weakest part: the T303 T305 batch had one green run and no repair, yet 3.9 of its 4.9 min books as blocking, while the GM said 'new tasks beginning is not something that blocks on it.' His third message, though, is an expectation that ends in 'Right?', not a rule that the line must read zero. (l) allows stated defaults at about 90% accuracy. Building his expected answer into the default would rig the instrument to agree with him and defeat its purpose, which is to find where the bottlenecks are. The plan calls the rule a knob and not a target, says what most of the line rests on, and names it the first knob to turn. The first measurement (24.8 of 27.9 min blocking) runs against his expectation and rests on default (a). That is a difference to report, not a defect.

decisions.summary: When a batch's own landing run is in flight, a wait is booked to that run, whatever else in flight ends later. This moves 12.1 min out of wait loops.
decisions.why: This fixes a wrong outcome as it was found. A builder's leftover loop was booked as the cause of a session's wait on a gate. Minutes are unchanged by the fix.

decisions.summary: The task line's four booking faults, and a fifth target name found: a main session's background command under the mark alone belongs to no task; the session's own quick or done goes to the batch whose span holds it; the builder-* targets and make carry get named categories; a carry belongs to the carried task. prewarm is left to T316.
decisions.why: These are the task line's own items, each a stated default. The fifth target (make builder-trees) is the same fault class, fixed as it was found.

decisions.why: This is a suspicion still to be measured, not a known wrong outcome. The defect that was established, inside a batch, is fixed in this task. It narrows nothing in the T298 request.

decisions.why: The block names none of these as refusing a write to the tree, and they are outside T295's line. decisions.summary: Left unfixed and unfiled, reported only as candidates ('Found and left? none filed by this builder'): wrapper options (env -i git, sudo -u x git), xargs git and sh -c 'git ...' for every tree guard; a quoted "git" in the history and discard guards; a wrapper spelled by its path in the make detector; cargo in make-only and no-poll
decisions.why: These are the class T295's line names ('miss a spelling of the program they refuse'), in the guards T295 fixes. Each is a check letting through what it exists to refuse: sudo -u x git push -f or "git" push -f past the history guard, sh -c 'git worktree add ...' past builder-pool, a backgrounded cargo past FR-008's no-poll refusal. The census lead-in, 'none serving a refusal of a tree write', is false for every item in this group. Item 1 and the first table row claim that 'every spelling' is refused. FR-009 requires a deferred defect to state why it is not fixed in this task, its filed task id and its order, and the section gives none of them. The ground offered, that the coordinating session's brief says not to file, is a session's instruction and not the GM's: the block itself says no GM words bear on the design. None of MODE 1's grounds applies: these fixes are not impossible, nothing in the request implies them, and fixing them does not defeat its purpose. Remedy, either one: fix them in T295; or have the coordinating session file them and restate this item with, for each one, why it is not fixed here, its filed task id and its order ('lands before ...'), and correct the lead-in sentence and the 'every spelling' claims.

decisions.summary: When the bundle names no tree (one built before T257), the hold uses the call's tree
decisions.why: Bundles built before T257 cannot name a tree, and this keeps their behavior as it was.

decisions.summary: Accepted: a builder's shell write of its worktree's held section, from a call whose cwd is the clone, is neither refused nor written back
decisions.why: Ruled on the outcome. Before D3 this case was never protected: it was judged against the wrong tree, and the clone was written into. D3 removes that wrong write, and nothing that worked before stops working. The outcome the hold protects, a verdict recorded only against the text that was reviewed, is still held, because make plan-verdict refuses a section that changed while it was reviewed. What is left costs time and produces no wrong outcome. That is why this ruling differs from the census items, which let bad work through.

decisions.summary: static-runs reads its crate delta in the work tree of the directory where the command's first make static or make closing-checks runs (following the walk's cds), else the clone. The message says what it measured.
decisions.why: It ends item 12's wrong outcome: a builder whose task had edited crates was told it changes no crate and to use make quick. This makes FR-007's 'crates the task's delta changes' true.

decisions.summary: The make static count stays in the clone's log: one count per task (T14), calls filed in the clone (T74)
decisions.why: It keeps FR-007's per-task count where T14 and T74 put it. Nothing that was asked is narrowed.

decisions.summary: make -C <dir> is not read: its crates are taken from the clone's tree, as before
decisions.why: For make -C <worktree> static or closing-checks, item 12's wrong outcome comes back unchanged: crates are edited, the builder is told there are none, and it is sent to make quick. make -C <tree> is how this project runs a target in another tree; the bundle's own MANIFEST records its verdict that way (451 T257). 'The walk does not read it' and 'as before' are reasons of implementation cost, not one of MODE 1's grounds, and the census does not list this form. Remedy, either one: read -C <dir> (D2's make detector already parses the make call), or carry it as a found-and-left defect with FR-009's why, filed task id and order.

decisions.summary: Seeding a new pool tree's build cache from a warm one is declined, with its measurement (260.1 s cold vs 187.9 s seeded) and a reopen condition
decisions.why: The follow-up asks to seed from a FREE warm tree. The block says make_cold is reached only when take found no free tree, so a free donor cannot exist at the moment a seed would run. A seed would copy a held tree's live cache, and its tool/ could carry a held tree's uncommitted sources. That makes the literal ask impossible in the one case it targets. Separately, one cold tree in about 35 hours of pool life makes the measured saving negligible against the request's purpose of throughput. The disk clause (3.3 GB against a 100 GB budget) is NOT relied on, because the GM's 2026-11-26 principle puts time saved above disk usage. The decline stands without that clause. blocks: ### T298 (the task line's count, observed 2026-11-26, method: the day's report as the coordinating session read it: a day's task time report was 2,294 lines in 38 per-task tables with no table of the window, the GM had to remember the period to ask for, and a batch landing's gate was booked to whichever of its tasks the mark or the command line named)

decisions.summary: The report opens with one table of the window (minutes, blocking, each as a percentage of the working time) and one line per landed task; builder minutes are the builder's event-log span.
decisions.why: This is how the report is laid out. It keeps T243's percentages of working time ((i)) and the breakdown the GM asked for. The table and the lines are the coordinating session's task-line words, and they narrow nothing he asked.

decisions.summary: Every make land is a batch keyed (feature, 'second tier: <tasks>'), owned by no task, with one category in the window table and its own section of one line per batch.
decisions.why: This is the GM's second message nearly word for word: 'move batched landing stuff that happens as the second tier of checks into its own separate category rather than counting it against any individual task.' Under the two-tier trial a single-task make land is also the second tier, so keying every landing as a batch matches his words.

decisions.summary: A task's own table ends at its make carry, found through the pool's log. With no carry found it ends where the batch's first attempt starts, a labeled GUESS knob (Batch::from).
decisions.why: This puts the GM's second message into effect: the second tier's time is not counted against a task. The fallback is a stated default of the kind (l) allows ('it doesn't have to be 100% exact'), and it is labeled where it is used.

decisions.summary: GUESS defaults for the second tier's blocking. A gate blocks nothing while any task's own blocking work is in flight. It blocks the batch (never a task) (a) when the session waits on it alone, (b) when it runs in the foreground, and (c) through a repair. A builder dispatched with Blocks: none leaves the gate waited on alone.
decisions.why: Each part was judged on its own. (c) A repair stops the batch from landing until the repair is done, which is (l)'s 'waiting on it to be done before it can be started' exactly. (b) A foreground run holds the session's next step by construction. (a) This is the weakest part: the T303 T305 batch had one green run and no repair, yet 3.9 of its 4.9 min books as blocking, while the GM said 'new tasks beginning is not something that blocks on it.' His third message, though, is an expectation that ends in 'Right?', not a rule that the line must read zero. (l) allows stated defaults at about 90% accuracy. Building his expected answer into the default would rig the instrument to agree with him and defeat its purpose, which is to find where the bottlenecks are. The plan calls the rule a knob and not a target, says what most of the line rests on, and names it the first knob to turn. The first measurement (24.8 of 27.9 min blocking) runs against his expectation and rests on default (a). That is a difference to report, not a defect.

decisions.summary: When a batch's own landing run is in flight, a wait is booked to that run, whatever else in flight ends later. This moves 12.1 min out of wait loops.
decisions.why: This fixes a wrong outcome as it was found. A builder's leftover loop was booked as the cause of a session's wait on a gate. Minutes are unchanged by the fix.
